claim.contributor: Boyle et al. (2008): DNase I hypersensitivity mapping by sequencing and tiled arrays
claim.earlier_demonstration: Primary abstract, PMID 18243105: mapped DNase I hypersensitive sites in human primary CD4+ T cells with high-throughput sequencing and whole-genome tiled arrays; the combined map contained 94,925 sites. claim.limitation_addressed: The seed describes high input and separate, time-consuming epigenomic workflows generally. A limitation measured specifically against this R4 implementation is not established.
claim.reported_gain: A seed gain attributable to R4 or a head-to-head comparison with its combined sequencing/array implementation is not established.
claim.tradeoffs_and_transfer_limits: DNase cleavage and Tn5 adapter insertion are different transformations; CD4+ primary cells and the seed GM12878 validation samples also differ. claim.contributor: Adey et al. (2010): Nextera/Tn5 fragmentation with adapter incorporation and PCR library construction
claim.earlier_demonstration: Primary full text, PMID 21143862: characterized hyperactive Tn5 with free synthetic mosaic-end adapters, coupling target-DNA fragmentation to joining adapters to target 5-prime ends; limited-cycle PCR appended platform-specific sequences. Experiments used purified genomic DNA, including human DNA, and sequenced the resulting libraries. Separate extensions included very low DNA input and a distinct PCR-free branch. Its Figure 4 discusses a homodimer acting on a duplicated 9-bp region; that is the insertion-geometry precedent the seed cites for read-offset interpretation.
claim.seed_design_change: The seed explicitly attributes prior tagmentation to R11, supporting adoption of the coupled fragmentation/adapter-tagging component and its PCR-compatible output. The coordinated seed change applies that reaction to native unfixed eukaryotic nuclei and uses accessibility-dependent sampling as the measurement. The seed also reports monitored PCR, omission of pre-PCR purification at low cell input and avoidance of size selection; specific inheritance of those choices from R11 is not established.
claim.limitation_addressed: R11 replaces separate fragmentation, end processing and adapter ligation in shotgun library preparation. The seed combines assay selection with adapter insertion to simplify accessibility-library generation. Calling every removed conventional step a directly inherited before-side operation would exceed the supplied extraction.
claim.reported_gain: R11 reports a 5-minute fragmentation/tagging reaction, comparable overall genomic coverage bias to conventional libraries, and over 2 million uniquely mapped read pairs from 10 pg human DNA with reduced complexity. The seed demonstrates accessibility profiling from 500–50,000 cells, reports DNase correlations of 0.79/0.83 and diminished sensitivity at smaller inputs. These are measurements of different workflows; the fraction of ATAC gain caused by this component alone is not established. Seed authors explain efficiency by coupling assay and library construction, without a component-ablation experiment.
claim.tradeoffs_and_transfer_limits: Purified genomic DNA and native nuclei differ materially. R11 sequence bias, size constraints and low-input DNA performance cannot be transferred quantitatively to chromatin. The seed uses Illumina transposase and custom Nextera PCR primers; exact equality of its loaded oligonucleotides, proprietary enzyme variant, buffer or full chemical end structure to R11 is not established. R11 PCR-free full-adapter/nick-translation chemistry is a separate branch, not evidence that ATAC used it. The seed 9-bp-derived mapping offsets are analysis context, not a new diagram operation.

claim.seed_design_change: The seed explicitly uses prior in vivo insertion as the rationale for its hypothesis that purified prokaryotic Tn5 acting on small numbers of unfixed nuclei could probe accessibility. It changes transposon/enzyme, biological system, reaction environment and payload to an in vitro sequencing-adapter assay.
claim.limitation_addressed: The demonstrated dependence of Hermes targeting on chromatin makes an accessibility-sensitive transposition assay plausible. A historical motive or seed limitation beyond the stated hypothesis is not established.
claim.reported_gain: The primary abstract measures an association for Hermes. The seed reports sensitive accessibility profiles, but no measured gain from transferring the Hermes principle or controlled cross-enzyme transfer experiment is established.
claim.tradeoffs_and_transfer_limits: Hermes is not Tn5. Yeast in vivo insertions and purified yeast genomic-DNA controls are not purified Tn5 reactions on native human nuclei. claim.contributor: Simon et al. (2012): FAIRE isolation and sequencing protocol benchmark
claim.earlier_demonstration: Primary full text, PMID 22262007: formaldehyde fixation, sonication and phenol/chloroform partitioning enrich DNA weakly crosslinked to protein. The protocol begins with 1–50 million cells, ideally 10 million, and schedules input-control preparation and FAIRE preparation over three days with overnight incubations. Sequencing library guidance includes purification, PCR and size selection.
claim.seed_design_change: The seed compares that workflow with native unfixed-nuclei Tn5 insertion and PCR. It removes the need for FAIRE crosslink-based partitioning in its own assay and couples accessibility sampling with adapter delivery. It does not adopt the FAIRE chemical isolation component.
claim.limitation_addressed: Seed authors describe multistep accessibility workflows as potentially loss-prone and slow. R14 independently documents its workflow schedule and recommended input; that establishes a benchmark, not a measured causal explanation for high input.
claim.reported_gain: R14 states its procedure can be completed in three days; its timing table contains two overnight stages. The seed reports low-input ATAC and a 275-minute blood-to-library/sequencing workflow in its own application. These are different workflow contexts, not a controlled speed or efficiency ratio against R14. Quantitative gain due specifically to eliminating crosslink reversal is not established.
claim.tradeoffs_and_transfer_limits: FAIRE chemical partitioning and Tn5 insertion have different selectivity. R14 itself reports shared and unique elements relative to DNase, so one assay cannot be assumed to recover all of another's features. The first overnight in the R14 schedule is for input-control DNA, the second for FAIRE DNA; its 1–50-million range is protocol guidance, not proof that no lower input could work. R14 does not supply a DNase library merely because the seed co-cites it in a DNase cell-input sentence.

High quality libraries from each cell type were sequenced on the Illumina platform to an average depth of 273 million uniquely mapping single-end tags.

While only a subset of these motif instances (2,351) coincided with high-confidence footprints, the vast majority of NRF1 motif instances in DNaseI footprints (89%) overlapped reproducible NRF1 ChIP-seq peaks (Fig. 1c).
